title: The magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts
content:
## 2.3 The magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts

### The shape and honesty of the FIELDWISE impact claim

FIELDWISE is a single-fellow, 30-month MSCA European Fellowship — a 24-month European Fellowship at HUN-REN ATK followed by a six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR — and its claim to impact is calibrated to that reality. It is deliberately a claim about methodological reach, credible magnitude context and a realistic uptake pathway, not a claim about immediate market penetration or a headline percentage of water saved. The importance of the contribution lies precisely in that discipline: FIELDWISE quantifies what it actually controls and delivers, and frames wider magnitude through published evidence and official statistics rather than invented figures, so that every number an evaluator reads is either measured by the project or referenced to a named source. This is what makes the impact assessment trustworthy at the magnitude it does claim, and it is the reason the contribution is durable beyond the funded period rather than rhetorical within it. The subsections below take the three impact dimensions in turn — scientific, agricultural/environmental and technological/economic, together with European and societal relevance — and for each give both the mechanism (how the result makes a difference beyond the immediate scope) and the magnitude (how large and how important that difference credibly is).

### Scientific impact and its magnitude

The project's primary scientific contribution is a validation framework in which operationally obtainable data streams are judged against independent plant-level ground truth and challenged under both unseen-year and new commercial-field conditions. It clarifies which stress relationships survive the transition from proximal measurements toward UAV and Sentinel-2 field monitoring, and which components of the modelling and decision workflow are genuinely reusable beyond the development crop — a methodological basis for later crop-by-crop extension across irrigated high-value horticulture rather than an unsupported universalisation from tomato. The magnitude of this contribution is amplified, and made portable to other research groups, by two engineered and citable outputs: the model card released within D2.1 Primary model, benchmark and model card, which reports the primary model and nonlinear benchmark with calibration, uncertainty, interpretability and blocked unseen-year performance; and the crop-transfer specification released within D2.2 Spectral/UAV/Sentinel harmonisation, scaling and crop-transfer specification, which enumerates the transferable core components, crop-specific parameters, minimum validation data and recalibration gates required to add a new crop. The prospectively measured transfer gap reported in D3.2 Prospective transferability, uncertainty and limited-recalibration report is itself a scientific result — the transfer loss is stated, not hidden — and it directly strengthens the R&I capacity, output and knowledge transfer of the participating organisations. Beyond the immediate scope, the importance of this work is that it confronts a systemic weakness in agricultural sensing and modelling: strong retrospective accuracy that does not survive leakage-safe temporal validation or prospective field testing, and that may diagnose established stress too late to alter irrigation. By demonstrating a parsimonious, interpretable and uncertainty-aware alternative and documenting exactly which relationships are reusable, FIELDWISE contributes a methodology other groups can adopt without depending on novel or opaque AI — a scientific magnitude that scales with reuse rather than being consumed by a single crop or site.

### Agricultural and environmental impact and its magnitude

FIELDWISE starts with processing tomato because the consortium can build on approximately five years of heterogeneous scientific observations (2022-2026); the intended application domain is irrigated high-value horticulture. The project deliberately will not promise a fixed percentage reduction in irrigation water, because actual savings depend on crop, cultivar, soil, weather, growth stage, irrigation system and the management action taken. To indicate credible magnitude without over-claiming, it anchors the potential to published processing-tomato evidence: comparable studies demonstrate water-saving effects in the approximate 8-30% range under specific strategies — for example, about 30% less irrigation water than empirical farmer management and about 7.5% less than ET-based scheduling in a two-year field trial (Carucci et al. 2023), and about 25% water saving from early-stage controlled deficit without statistically significant yield loss, with poorly timed or prolonged deficits reducing yield (Badr et al. 2026). These are bounded context, not project targets: FIELDWISE reports its own water saving, yield, quality and uncertainty from the prospective validation data rather than adopting any of these figures as a promise, and communication messaging is disciplined to avoid an unearned numeric water-saving claim. This restraint is itself important for impact. The project's environmental contribution — better-timed irrigation that serves SDG 2, SDG 6, SDG 12 and SDG 13 — is credible precisely because it is quantified from the project's own measurements and bounded by literature evidence in the plausible 8-30% band, and because the physiology- and plant-stage-aware timing premise on which it rests is exactly what the cited timing evidence supports. The magnitude that matters here is not a single percentage but the demonstrated ability to make water-yield trade-offs visible and to act on them earlier, which is the mechanism by which any real-world saving in the published range would be captured.

### Technological and economic impact and its magnitude

The web-based DrR MVP provides a tangible route from validated research to external testing (D4.1 Crop-configurable DrR web MVP with validated processing-tomato module), preserving the distinction between the fellow's pre-existing DrR background and FIELDWISE foreground. The architecture is crop-configurable: processing tomato supplies the first validated crop module, while the reusable data-ingestion, uncertainty, visualisation and irrigation-attention components can support later modules once crop-specific validation exists. The economic magnitude is deliberately not asserted as an invented EUR/ha figure; instead FIELDWISE quantifies irrigation water applied, water productivity, yield and marketable yield, quality indicators, intervention timing, warning lead time and operational requirements, from which later economic value can be assessed by those best placed to do so. The route to that value is concrete and is hardened by the non-academic placement: AgroVIR identifies the data, usability, interoperability and workflow requirements for future FMIS integration through D5.1 AgroVIR operational/interoperability assessment and D5.2 Post-MSCA FMIS integration and exploitation roadmap, while Krumatic supports software implementation and Bulgarian farmer-facing uptake. The importance of this pathway — its potential reach beyond the immediate scope — is indicated by the operational footprint of the industrial partner's platform: AgroVIR reports a farm-management information system in production use across more than 745,000 hectares in eight countries, including Hungary and Bulgaria, the two countries in which FIELDWISE works. A successful FMIS-integration route therefore targets an existing operational base rather than a hypothetical one, which is what gives a single-fellow technological result a plausible path to scale. The economic claim FIELDWISE makes is thus not a promised return but a credibly instrumented route to one, backed by the measured operational metrics the project actually delivers.

### European and societal relevance and its magnitude

The domain in which scientifically transferable, plant-based irrigation decision support could ultimately matter is large. Eurostat reports fresh vegetables cultivated over approximately 2.0 million hectares in the EU in 2023, and about 0.7 million EU farms cultivating fresh vegetables in the 2020 census — the scale of the horticultural application domain, stated explicitly as a potential domain and not as an immediate addressable market. Bulgaria supplies concrete downstream context for the project's cross-border reach: about 35.6 thousand hectares of main vegetable-production area and about 128 thousand tonnes of tomato in harvest 2024. The combination of Hungarian scientific and industrial environments, a real commercial-farmer validation setting, Bulgarian software and dissemination links through Krumatic, and a defined post-MSCA replication and transferability route through MVCRI provides a realistic pathway toward wider reuse. The magnitude claimed here is honest about horizon: FIELDWISE does not assert that it will irrigate two million hectares, but that it produces the scientifically controlled, documented transfer methodology and the operational evidence needed for the approach to be reused within a domain of that size, and it names the specific channels — industrial (AgroVIR), cross-border software (Krumatic) and institutional replication (MVCRI) — through which that reuse would proceed. This is the societal importance of the work: addressing water scarcity and climatic variability in European high-value horticulture through decision support whose reach is anchored in real production statistics rather than aspiration.

### Magnitude versus importance: why the contribution matters beyond its immediate scope

The three impact dimensions share one design logic that determines both their magnitude and their importance. Their magnitude within the fellowship is modest and honestly bounded — a single validated crop module, one instrumented commercial field, one MVP evaluated by one industrial partner, water-saving potential expressed only as literature-referenced context. Their importance beyond the fellowship is disproportionately larger, because what FIELDWISE delivers is reusable: a validation methodology, a documented reusable-versus-crop-specific separation, a quantified transfer gap, an openly released model card and crop-transfer specification, and a named integration and replication route. Each of these is engineered to be picked up and extended by others, so the contribution compounds rather than terminates at project end. This is reinforced at the human-capital level: the action consolidates the fellow as an Agricultural Data Scientist specialised in plant stress, Earth observation and decision support (a profile carried by the agreed Career Development Plan and the inter-sectoral placement), sustaining the capacity to carry the work forward. Finally, the credibility of the whole impact claim rests on its instrumentation: eleven KPIs each measure something the project controls and delivers, and none promises a numeric water saving in advance. FIELDWISE therefore offers evaluators a rare combination — a genuinely important scientific, environmental and economic contribution whose every magnitude statement is either measured by the project or transparently referenced — and it is this combination of reach and restraint, rather than any single quantified figure, that constitutes the project's contribution to the expected impacts.
